for you to get your mind
around doing PCBs?
And the reason I ask is
because, you know, a lot of engineers,
they don't get any exposure
to printed circuit boards like at all,
and they just do everything in schematics.

that transition from,

you know, what a schematic is

professors talking about

- Hello everyone. Welcome to
the Altium OnTrack podcast.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today we are talking with three students
from the University of Minnesota,
Alexander Wan, Kevin Vo, and Ethan Chung.

They are part of the Bright
Manufacturing Challenge.

They've completed their
phase one of the challenge

and I'm very excited to
talk to them today about

what they're doing as part
of Bright Manufacturing.

Guys, thank you so much
for joining us today.

- [Participant] Thank
you for having us, Zach.
- Yeah, absolutely.

Okay, so we're setting new
records here all the time
because just recently we had
our youngest guest on the show.
And I know you guys are our competitors

for also being the youngest
guests on the show,

but there's also three of
you on the same episode.

So we're setting records
around here all the time.
I'm really interested

to know more about the Bright
Manufacturing challenge,

but first if each of you
could just take a moment
to introduce yourselves to our audience.
- Yeah, I'm Ethan.

I go to the University
of Minnesota Twin Cities
and I major in electrical engineering

and I'm going into my
sophomore year this semester.

- My name is Kevin, I go
to the same school as Ethan
and I'm a mechanical engineer.
I going to the same year as Ethan.

- Alex is also majoring
in electrical engineering

and he's also going to the
University of Minnesota

and he's also going into
the same year as us as well.
- Okay. We have Alex on the line here.

Hopefully his internet will
improve, so we can talk
with him a little bit, but that's great.
We've got all three of you here.
So if you could tell us a little bit
about the Bright Manufacturing Challenge

and I just for a little
bit of background here,

the three of you were introduced
to me from Terra Dunn,
who is also one of our podcast guests,
in fact she was on earlier this year.

And SMTA was also involved
in this challenge.

So if you could give us a
little bit of background.

- Yeah, so the Bright
Manufacturing Challenge
is basically a challenge where teams

of students from different
universities design, create
and program a robot from the ground up.
And this challenge we were tasked
with building a line following robot,

which is basically a robot that
can follow a pre-made track

that consists of black
lines that we follow
and a white background.

And then what we did was
we had to design PCBs,
create 3D models of the robot

and then we also have to plan
for firmware integration.
- So solidly multidisciplinary approach
to this manufacturing challenge.

So it's called the Bright
Manufacturing Challenge right?
And what's the end application
for what you guys are building?

- I think one of the main
things that it's teaching us
to do is how to,

or it's showing us how
to go through the process
of engineering.
Like we start with a schematic

and then we follow all
the steps towards reaching
the final manufactured product.
- Okay so how did you all decide
that you wanna participate in this?
And part of the reason I ask is
because, you know, I've talked to
some young people in the past,
folks who skew a little younger
and are just getting into electronics
and they don't often get into
electronics purely from the
electrical engineering perspective.
Sometimes they kind of stumble into it

because they went into,
you know, programming

and then embedded and
then that's how they get

into things like electronics
engineering and PCB design.
So if you give us the overview,

why did you wanna participate
in this competition?
- I mean for us it's like we wanted
to improve our PCB design

and since we're going
into our sophomore year,

we didn't have any classes
to like go into like how
to design and like process
and like go through the, you know,

the general processes and we
just joined this competition
because it looks kind of fun to do,

and this, you know,
challenge to work together

as like a team across
multi disciplinary groups.

- Right so Kevin, you're
coming in from the mechanical
perspective and then Ethan

and I believe Alexander
you're both coming at
from the electrical perspective.
How did you guys initially get started?
Kevin, was it you driving the form factor
from the mechanical design side
or were you accommodating what Ethan

and Alex were doing from
the electrical side?

- I was more of like the person
who was accommodating them
'cause like for them, they're just,

for this first round it's just
like them designing the PCBs
and then researching the components
to make past the first round.
And I'm just there to

see if I could like
integrate their components
into the robot itself.
- So at the end of the day, you all have
to manufacture a physical robot, right?
So what are the processes you're using
on the mechanical side?
Are you doing like 3D printing?
Are you ordering off the shelf stuff?
What are you doing there?
- For me, I'm 3D printing
or doing some 3D modeling like Onshape
for Ethan and Alex.
I think you can take over Ethan.

- Yeah, so we were given
a base like chassis
that was made out of a PCB,

and then we had to come up
with an additional feature

and then that additional feature
would determine like what

3D model designs that
we would want to add to

our robot to make it function
with the additional feature.
So for example, we have,
if I could share my screen really quick.
- Sure, sure.

And we have some folks that
that are listening on audio
and if they wanna see a model

of everything you guys have
built, they should head on over
to YouTube and take a look at the episode.
Okay, go ahead.
- [Ethan] All right, so Kevin, Alex
and I designed a CAD model in Onshape,
which features our robot that we designed.

And then basically what we
have here is the chassis,
which is composed of a PCB,
and then we nail some motors, wheels,

and then right here at the
back of the, at the back
of the robot is our additional feature.

And then to install
this additional feature,

we had to add 3D printed parts
completely designed by Kevin,
which will help our encoders work.

And our encoders will
basically help our robot drive
straight so we don't drift off the line
and have any other mistakes
while we're driving at the competition.
- [Zach] So this additional feature,
this is what a motor control board
that senses the encoders essentially.

- Yeah.
- Okay. Okay.
So before doing all of this,
had anybody on the team ever
designed a printed circuit board?
- Yeah, me and Alex in particular,
we've worked on a few different PCBs.
So none of them were class related.
They were all based on personal projects
that we thought were interesting
or on extracurricular club activities.

For example IEEE and
they weren't too complex.
They all stick to like the fundamentals
but they definitely helped us get familiar
with the Altium software

and get us prepared
for like the challenges
that this like event would pose.

- Okay so you had to go
through the whole process
of talking to fabricators, making sure
that you are within their capabilities,
those kinds of tasks.
- [Ethan] Yeah, exactly.
- How how difficult was it for you
to get your mind around doing PCBs,

and the reason I ask is because
you know, a lot of engineers

they don't get any exposure
to printed circuit boards

like at all and they just
do everything in schematics.

And as a result, I think that
transition from you know,
what a schematic is supposed to look like
versus what a PCB is supposed
to look like can be kind of difficult.

- Yeah. It was definitely
a learning process.
We had to reference like a lot

of different YouTube
videos including yours,
which are amazing.
And we also had to go

through like multiple
professors talking about
how like best PCB practices,

what like design rules we should
follow, that sort of thing.

And honestly on our first
PCB that we manufactured,
a lot didn't go as expected,

but that is expected for a
lot of things that you start

for the first time,
especially with something
as multidimensional as PCB design.
- So what exactly didn't go as expected?
I'm really interested to hear this one,
because I think the experience is a
little different for everybody.

- Yeah so some things that
we didn't take into account
for on our original board were like
some nuances in like documentation.

Documentation is actually
a big thing that we have

to look out for because
there's so much depth
and complexity to a lot

of the integrated circuit
components that we use.

And for example, one of the
ones that caused us a lot

of trouble was
microcontroller documentation.

So some like
misinterpretations of the word

or of the instructions
on how to use it led to

the microcontroller
not working as intended

and then it just led the
entire project downhill.

So we had to fix that and
create a second board.
But we hope that it will turn out well

'cause that's still a project
we're working on currently.
- So you mentioned that

there were no PCB design classes
at your university right?

You kind of left to, to jump
in and just figure it out.
Despite there not being any PCB design
classes offered at your university,

do you still think the
rest of your curriculum
prepared you adequately to be able
to get into PCB design software

and start working with
a printed circuit board?
- From my experience, I haven't taken

as many upper level
electrical engineering classes
that would prepare you for PCB design.

But I know that my
university will offer those
after I complete my general requirements
and my prerequisites for those classes.

And that will mostly come
during junior and senior year.

I've talked to a couple of
electrical engineers that
are studying at the U of M

and they said that the classes
were pretty high quality
and that they should help with PCB design,

but I still have yet to experience
those classes for myself.
- [Zach] Okay. Okay.
Well you're taking the approach that

I took learning PCB design
I guess, which is just
to dive in and figure it out.

- Yeah.
- Kevin, with you being
the mechanical person on the team,
I'm a little interested to know here

because I was not taking
mechanical engineering courses
when I was at university.
What was your take on that question?

Do you think your coursework
adequately prepared you

to anticipate what you would
have to accommodate in a PCB?

- Personally, I have not
experienced those classes
to prepare me for these,
but it's just, I did like
personal projects back in my high school

and like we had an
opportunity to like do Onshape
and like do 3D printing.

So I was well prepared
to accommodate for them.

But in this university,
there is no specific class
for doing cadding I believe,

or I'm not, I don't have the
prerequisites for it yet.
- Okay. Okay.

So I think another question
here related to all this
with the PCB design and production,

what were the gotchas in
the thing that you built?

What were the things
that you didn't realize
kind of came outta left field

and you needed to plan
for it ahead of time,

but you just didn't know
about it when you were
still doing the design?

- I'd say it was definitely
looking at the layer stack up
'cause what we did
for our additional feature PCB

was create a flex rigid
PCB and the flex rigid PCB
or the flex portion of the PCB
and the rigid portion of the PCB
have very different stack ups.

So we forgot to account for
that in our initial like
test run of the design.

And then once we looked
it over, we found out
that the stackups had to be different.
So it took Alex a lot of time
and research to find out what the correct
and most optimal stackup would be.
But once we got that figured out,
it was smooth sailing from there.

- So did you get any, like
did you try to put this in
with a fabrication house

and then they told you
you needed to change it
or were you going through the design

and then midway through the
design you started looking at it
and saying, is this correct?
We need to do some research?

- [Ethan] Yeah, it was
definitely the latter.

- Okay, well I guess that's
better than, you know,

sending an offer for
manufacturing thinking you did

everything perfectly and
then all of a sudden, right?

- Yeah.
- Absolutely.

So what were some of the
resources that you found

that were really helpful for
getting started on the PCBs
that you're working on and then
ultimately getting them completed?

- I think one of the biggest
things that we've learned

to use resource wise was LLMs
like ChatGPT and Perplexity

'cause they really
streamline the data sheet,
like searching process,
like the part searching, all of that.
And it also like in some cases it can help

with verifying like schematic
parts of your design.

Like saying which pin
should be connected to what,

as long as you make sure that
it references the data sheet.

Something else that we looked
into a lot was just like
YouTube videos in general.

Like when starting something
new like a flex rigid PCB

design for the first time,
referencing YouTube was
I think a very big help for us

'cause it showed us what we
knew, what we didn't know,
what we could have researched more
and a ton of other things like that.
- Yeah and I gotta agree.
When I'm trying to learn something new,

I'm definitely someone who
will go to YouTube just

because it's always nice to
be able to see it right there
and it makes it much more tangible.
Did you leverage any like books?

Did you have any mentors
that helped you with this?
- So we have two other people on our team,
and one of them is a, I believe
senior education vice at the U of M
in electrical engineering.

And he was really a big help
on getting some of our like
more general PCB design questions answered

that like focused more
on our specific design
'cause he has a lot of experience

and he was one of the people
that actually prompted us

to join this challenge,
so we could help like

increase our PCB like
knowledge and skill I guess.

And it was a really big
help like showing us
what we could do better.
- Okay yeah, that's always helpful
to have somebody review the design.

And I say that as someone
who gets often asked

to do design reviews, as
I'm sure you guys are aware.

So do you guys have the
design here with you today?
Do you wanna do a live walkthrough?

- Yeah, of course.
- Okay. Let's take a look.

- [Ethan] So we are in the
Altium software right now
and I will quickly run you through
each of the schematics that we have.

So schematics 3, 4, 5,
and 6 are all pre-made

by the people that run the
Bright Manufacturing Challenge,
and then they give us freedom of design
for the additional feature.
So this is what we spend 90%
of our time on the challenge on
'cause we had to go come up with an idea,

we had to put this idea
into the schematic form

and then we also had to create
an additional PCB for it.

- [Zach] Okay. And let's
see what that looks like.

- Yeah.
- So actually before,

before we get too deep
into that, so you said some
of the schematics were already pre-made.

- Yeah.
- Did you have,
you had to do your own layout
for those schematics?

- [Ethan] Yeah, I could
run through that first too.

- [Zach] Gotcha okay. Yeah,
let's go ahead and do that.
Let's see what you put together.

- [Ethan] So this is our
design for the main chassis

and the chassis is made
of the PCB of course.
So at the front of the robot,

we have our infrared sensors
which detects the black

or which areas are black
and which areas are white.
So then the robot can follow on the track.
And then this center here is
where the microcontroller is housed.
There's a bunch of like, yeah, sorry,
there's like decoupling capacitors.

We have devices that
control the IR sensors

and then a bunch more
in this middle center.

And then closer to the
back, we have a bunch
of the power circuitry,
and this is where we attach a battery
and connect it to the power circuitry.

And then it provides
the motor with powers,
which is this section right here.

And then it also provides
the rest of the IC
with powers as well.

And then you-
- Okay, sorry,
so just if you could,

do you wanna zoom in on the
power section just a little bit?

- Yeah, sure.
- See what that looks like.

So it looks like you have
probably multiple rails here

or maybe a couple of
power supplies in parallel
near the wheels, is that correct?
- [Ethan] Yeah, we have a,

the wheels are supplied
with positive five volts

and then as we go farther
down, we step it down
to 3.3 volts for the IR sensors.

And then, yeah, Alex did
most of the power schematics
or no power layouts.

So if he was here he'd like
be a lot more knowledgeable
to talk about it but...
- [Zach] Yeah, it looks like dropped off

due to his internet
connection, but that's fine.
Okay so yeah, so I see some power routing,
I see some polygons.

It looks like you have a
decent size inductor there
kind of in the center.

So you're probably bringing
in looks like five volts
and then you step it down
to 3.3 volts with the switching regulator.

- Yeah.
- Is that the approach?

- Yep.
- Okay. Okay.

And then this goes over
to your microcontroller
and then you've probably got LED driver
or just an IR sensor?
I guess this would be an IR sensor.

- [Ethan] Yeah, we have
a total of six IR sensors

lined up at the front of the
robot, which is around here.

And then that's what
detects the changes in color
for the track.
- [Zach] Got it. Okay.
So everybody did their own custom PCB
with these preset schematics,

and then you have your
additional feature PCB.

So I'd be interested to see
a walkthrough of that design.

- Sure.
- Okay. Let's take a look.

- [Ethan] This PCB mainly
focused on having features
that would help the robot drive straight
or use something called dead reckoning.

Dead reckoning, which is
it takes in environmental

conditions and then it spits
out like whether or not

like you should turn your
wheel a bit to correct

for some slight mechanical
error in the motors for example.

And so to do that, we added
two magnetic encoders on
the sides right here, U8 and U7.

And then in the center right
here is an IMU, which will,
it houses a gyroscope

and an accelerometer so we
can track how far it turns
whenever it turns,

and we could also track how
much it accelerates basically.
- [Zach] Okay. Okay.

And then this was I guess the
smaller PCB that you showed

or earlier in there, in
the 3D model I should say

that was basically mounted
like up above the wheels.

- Exactly, yeah.
- Okay.

- [Ethan] And sorry, I
made one small mistake.
This right here is the IMU

and this large one is a
secondary microcontroller
that we have for processing the data
and sending it back to the main board.
- [Zach] Okay, so I have to ask,

why didn't you leverage the
existing MCU in the other board?

Was it because you're just
not allowed to modify that?

- Exactly.
- I ask because
maybe you could have put for example,
a connector right?

Send the signal back
down, send it back up,
or were you just not allowed to do that?
- [Ethan] We weren't allowed to do that.

One of the requirements for
the additional feature was

that it sent like, it
only had one function.
So if we sent individual encoder
and IMU data to the main board MCU,
then that would've violated the rule
of having one additional feature
that would count as two.

So what we did was we've
made a whole new board
and then we put its own MCU on it,
so that it would only send position data

and then we could also
show off the flex feature

of this PCB if we go into
3D mode really quickly.
So this is what it looks like in 3D mode.

And then once we press
five on the keyboard,
it shows the PCB flexed.
- [Zach] So why did you have the PCB done
like this specifically?

Is it because those chips
on the edges kind of need

to face towards the wheel
in order to function?
- [Ethan] Yeah, let me go to the CAD
to help me explain this.

How the magnetic encoders
work is they need
to be perpendicular

or they need to be facing
a magnet that spins along

with the wheel axle so that
it can record that data
and send it to the microcontroller.
So we had to have the PCB perpendicular
to the axle so that we can attach a magnet
to the axle so that when it spins,
the encoder could record it.

And then we thought that
the best way to do this was

through a flex rigid PCB that
could be mounted like this.

- Yeah, and I like that
you've brought in the model
of the PCB here with the bend,

because now it's really clear
why you have the little flex
wings there on the side.

It sits right over the
top of the existing board.
Okay okay. Very nice.
So I think now is a good time for you

to maybe reflect on this as
far as a learning experience.
What would you do differently

or would you do anything
differently when it comes to
the PCB design or the mechanical design?

What do you think, what
would you do differently
in this design?

- PCB wise, I think I'd
stay farther away from

four layer flex PCB boards
'cause they get really pricey.
When we sent in our flex PCB for a quote,

we were expecting it around
the range of, I don't know,
somewhere around $200.
But then it came back
and the PCB itself was $680 for one.

So I think that if we do
do something like this

in the future, we'd either
use like JST connectors
to connect the encoders on the side
to the MCU on the main board,

or we just have like, I
don't know, we come up

with something better than
a four layer flex PCP board.

- Kevin, what do you
think, is there anything

that could be done differently
to maybe optimize the design
at least from the mechanical aspect?
- Yeah, we didn't, if we go back

or if you refer back to like
the 3D modeling, like CAD,
we haven't put in the battery itself

because they gave us a
battery and it's huge.

So I need to still kind
of work around having

that huge battery bouncing
all over the robot yeah.
- I see, I see okay. Both good points.

What would your be approach
be to deal with the battery?

- My, because since it's like
really huge, to be honest,
it's like as big as a robot itself.
I was just think of like Velcroing it

and just like ignore and
hope that it just stays on.
But if I need to put,

because the more weight
I put on the robot,
the slower the robot goes.
So I don't want to like

make the inefficiencies
for the power yeah.
- Sure. Sure.
And then I suppose if you maybe put
that battery in the wrong location,

it's gonna push too
much on one of the axles
while you don't push on the other axle
and so it could affect how it drives.

- Yeah, exactly.
- Okay. Okay.
Well guys, we are getting up here on time,

but I wanna thank you all
for coming on the show.
This is really great

to see young students getting
into electronics design
and just kind of jumping in with both feet
and learning as much as you can.

If you could, you've already
passed the first part
of the Bright Manufacturing Challenge.
Tell us what comes next.
- So the PCB step was stage one,

and we also just passed stage
two, which was the design
for manufacturing step.
So what we have left is round three,

which is the assembly round
where we create a prototype
of our robot.

And then lastly, we have
round four where all

of the finalists, which were
eight teams go to Chicago.

And then we test our
robots against each other

and see which robot can
complete the track the fastest.

- Very cool. I wish you
all the best of luck.
Hopefully you win.

We'll see if you complete
it to the fastest,
I'm sure Tara Dunn will, we will reach out
and let me know what the updates are

and of course you guys have
my contact info, make sure

to keep in touch with me
and let me know how it goes.

- Of course, of course.
- So Kevin, Alex

and Ethan, thank you so
much for being here today.

- [Ethan] Yeah, thank you
so much for having us.

- Absolutely; to everyone
that's out there listening,

we've been talking with
Alexander Wan, Kevin Vo
and Ethan Chung.

All of them are University
of Minnesota students

who are participating in the
Bright Manufacturing Challenge.
If you're watching on YouTube, make sure

to hit the like button,
hit the subscribe button.

You'll be able to keep up with
all of our podcast episodes
and tutorials as they come out.

And last but not least, don't
stop learning, stay on track
and we'll see you next time.
Thanks everybody.
(pleasant music)

title: Students Tackle PCB Design Challenge: From Schematic to Robot
